e-8249.knowledge_point: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Function by Finding Eigenvalues
e-8249.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+x_2^2+2x_3^2+4x_1x_2.$
e-8249.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/44753acffd8b6384cd291f9b0758edd7676acb319caa22d5b07be36dcf72a5a6.png)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,2,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/217b5d7d3b82800bdfc44d83ca8b068e02a37759e52b7a8382505bfb102f753f.png)

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3y_1^2 + 2y_2^2 - y_3^2.
$$

e-8250.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
e-8250.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2-2x_1x_2+2x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
e-8250.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/69dcf821f3ff202b567b901d8f512c5cecf7159617ca51a0664c14a5099e9715.png)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +3 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/fc9465d4e5bcd43a3c29e5946b05ec18cdbc7453a4011aa548f374016c561b45.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/59c1bd46325fab8a52fed162d7ae47e8fb33a10cc524cd770a3b18f5934e51dd.png)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/adc9241219f3b5ebce0d8418bf34e250b7230ea612fabca5bdfc109c98a18dbb.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/dcab437eb77b29ab5bcd5c3ae14b77f10f01382aafadf2aecded1bb1fb72dc32.png)

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/3f6b1002893290dde6c9a68425b0035e249ff3630a41d29c9da5756c1a18f6a6.png)

e-8251.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 3D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
e-8251.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/6135fe578745ebf2eccb4370557f0dba6ec27361a192e4e87536eadad87a39bf.png)

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
e-8251.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=4, \quad$ $\lambda_2=2, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/13eee082d48c56e6c7e796549eddc0185868b39841a7c5946ce9ce9e996ba553.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/1e7c81e373377bd719e1bbc9e87a8c88d13f6116bcf2949897fc26246e2265d1.png)

- For $\lambda_2=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/61311029da90b54253a552ce2198ce9193d7f343c3ab345eea25419444da00a3.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/3bf5334469b8b135548dfbd0c35725ee6927e2a169c6db37a1b0bae3f62695e5.png)

- For $\lambda_3=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/1cb1b34b0df191e9fa63a907ba59e26a2ad16f3977e97d5b8588dc5e51f2c3a0.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3  \| = 1,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/39bf82ed6be834f41140a70e048268b39d47d7a0944461247d312d4efe95d184.png)

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/fb5604c6dc892a34af523d6b9b769cd50c59e82ed65d7be47cb89ed6044125bf.png)

after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$

Question 1
?

Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of Q(x)=x12+x22+x32+4x1x3.

a
3y12+y32
b
y12+y22+y32
c
3y12+y22−y32
d
y12−y22
e
2y12−y22−y32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[102010201]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|1−λ0201−λ0201−λ|=0(1−λ)|1−λ221−λ|=0(1−λ)((1−λ)(1−λ)−4)=0(1−λ)(λ2−2λ−3)=0(1−λ)(λ−3)(λ+1)=0λ=3,1,−1

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

D=[30001000−1].

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

3y12+y22−y32.

content.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$

decision.explanation: The symmetric matrix is A = [[1,3],[3,1]]. Its characteristic equation is (1-λ)^2-9=0, giving eigenvalues 4 and -2. Thus the canonical form is 4y_1^2-2y_2^2.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
4{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.
$$

decision.explanation: The symmetric matrix is A = [[1,2],[2,1]]. Its characteristic equation is (1-λ)^2-4=0, giving eigenvalues 3 and -1. Orthogonal diagonalization therefore gives 3y_1^2-y_2^2.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}.
$$

y12

3y12+y22
e
3y12−y22

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1221]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|1−λ221−λ|=0(1−λ)(1−λ)−4=0λ2−2λ−3=0(λ−3)(λ+1)=0λ=3,−1

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

D=[300−1].

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

3y12−y22.

decision.explanation: The symmetric matrix is A = [[-1,2],[2,2]]. Its characteristic polynomial is (-1-λ)(2-λ)-4 = λ²-λ-6 = (λ-3)(λ+2). The eigenvalues are 3 and -2, so the canonical form is 3y_1²-2y_2².

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
3{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of Q(x)=x12+x22−x32−6x1x2.

a
y12−y22+2y32
b
4y12−y22−2y32
c
4y12−2y22
d
−y12−2y22−2y32
e
2y12+y22
Submit

decision.explanation: The symmetric matrix is A = [[1,-3,0],[-3,1,0],[0,0,-1]]. The upper 2×2 block has eigenvalues 4 and -2, and the remaining eigenvalue is -1. In descending order, orthogonal diagonalization gives 4y_1²-y_2²-2y_3².

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
4{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of Q(x)=x12+x22−x32−6x1x2.

a
y12−y22+2y32
b
4y12−y22−2y32
c
4y12−2y22
d
−y12−2y22−2y32
e
2y12+y22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−30−31000−1]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|1−λ−30−31−λ000−1−λ|=0(−1−λ)|1−λ−3−31−λ|=0(−1−λ)((1−λ)(1−λ)−9)=0(−1−λ)(λ2−2λ−8)=0(−1−λ)(λ−4)(λ+2)=0λ=4,−1,−2

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

D=[4000−1000−2].

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

4y12−y22−2y32.

content.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
4{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Question 6
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12−4x1x2+5x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[−1001] and P=[1001]
b
D=[3001] and P=[−12121212]
c
D=[6001] and P=[−15252515]
d
D=[300−2] and P=[−26262626]
e
D=[4002] and P=[−13232313]
Submit

decision.explanation: The matrix A = [[2,-2],[-2,5]] has eigenvalues 6 and 1. Corresponding unit eigenvectors are (-1,2)/√5 and (2,1)/√5. These orthonormal columns form the displayed P in option c, satisfying PᵀAP = D and giving Q = 6y_1²+y_2².

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =6,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 6
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=2x12−4x1x2+5x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[−1001] and P=[1001]
b
D=[3001] and P=[−12121212]
c
D=[6001] and P=[−15252515]
d
D=[300−2] and P=[−26262626]
e
D=[4002] and P=[−13232313]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[2−2−25]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|2−λ−2−25−λ|=0λ2−7λ+6=0λ=6,1

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=6, we have A−6I=[2−2−25]−6[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−6I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−12]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[−12].

  • For λ2=1, we have A−1I=[2−2−25]−1[1001]=[1−2−24]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−1I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[21]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[21].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[6001],P=[−15252515]

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option c. For A = [[2,-2],[-2,5]], the orthonormal vectors (-1,2)/√5 and (2,1)/√5 have eigenvalues 6 and 1, respectively. Thus PᵀP = I and PᵀAP = diag(6,1), giving Q = 6y_1²+y_2². The deliberately incorrect submission selected d.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =6,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=x12+12x1x2−4x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[800−5] and P=[15−252515]
b
D=[800−5] and P=[12−121212]
c
D=[500−8] and P=[313−213213313]
d
D=[8005] and P=[12−121212]
e
D=[500−8] and P=[−213313313213]
Submit

decision.explanation: A = [[1,6],[6,-4]] has characteristic polynomial λ²+3λ-40 = (λ-5)(λ+8). The vectors (3,2)/√13 and (-2,3)/√13 are orthonormal eigenvectors with eigenvalues 5 and -8, respectively. Thus option c satisfies PᵀAP = D, giving Q = 5y_1²-8y_2².

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -40 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-8)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]
$$

content.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -40 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,-8\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-8)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -8\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=−3x12+2x1x2−3x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[200−4] and P=[313−213213313]
b
D=[400−2] and P=[12−121212]
c
D=[−200−4] and P=[−25151525]
d
D=[4002] and P=[−213313313213]
e
D=[−200−4] and P=[12−121212]
Submit

decision.explanation: A = [[-3,1],[1,-3]] has orthonormal eigenvectors (1,1)/√2 and (-1,1)/√2 with eigenvalues -2 and -4, respectively. These are the columns of P in option e, so PᵀP = I and PᵀAP = D. The canonical form is -2y_1²-4y_2².

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=−3x12+2x1x2−3x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[200−4] and P=[313−213213313]
b
D=[400−2] and P=[12−121212]
c
D=[−200−4] and P=[−25151525]
d
D=[4002] and P=[−213313313213]
e
D=[−200−4] and P=[12−121212]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−311−3]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|−3−λ11−3−λ|=0λ2+6λ+8=0λ=−2,−4

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−311−3]−(−2)[1001]=[−111−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[11]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[11].

  • For λ2=−4, we have A−(−4)I=[−311−3]−(−4)[1001]=[1111]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−4)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[−11].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[−200−4],P=[12−121212]

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=14x12−6x1x2+6x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[1500−5] and P=[−25151525]
b
D=[500−15] and P=[310−110110310]
c
D=[15005] and P=[25−151525]
d
D=[500−15] and P=[12−121212]
e
D=[15005] and P=[−310110110310]
Submit

decision.explanation: A = [[14,-3],[-3,6]] has eigenvalues 15 and 5. The orthonormal vectors (-3,1)/√10 and (1,3)/√10 have these respective eigenvalues. Thus option e satisfies PᵀP = I and PᵀAP = diag(15,5), giving the canonical form 15y_1²+5y_2².

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}14-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +75 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =15,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=15,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-15I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]-15[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-15I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}15 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 9

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=14x12−6x1x2+6x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[1500−5] and P=[−25151525]
b
D=[500−15] and P=[310−110110310]
c
D=[15005] and P=[25−151525]
d
D=[500−15] and P=[12−121212]
e
D=[15005] and P=[−310110110310]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[14−3−3−6]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|14−λ−3−36−λ|=0λ2−20λ+75=0λ=15,5

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=15, we have A−15I=[14−3−36]−15[1001]=[−1−3−3−9]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−15I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−31]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=10, we get v1‖v1‖=110[−31].

  • For λ2=5, we have A−5I=[14−3−36]−5[1001]=[9−3−31]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[13]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get v2‖v2‖=110[13].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[15005],P=[−310110110310]

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}14-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +75 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =15,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=15,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-15I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]-15[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-15I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}15 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 10

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−6x1x2+9x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[10000] and P=[−110310310110]
b
D=[300−3] and P=[−15252515]
c
D=[9003] and P=[−15252515]
d
D=[5000] and P=[−12121212]
e
D=[5005] and P=[−12121212]
Submit

decision.explanation: A = [[1,-3],[-3,9]] has orthonormal eigenvectors (-1,3)/√10 and (3,1)/√10 with eigenvalues 10 and 0. These form the columns of P in option a, so PᵀAP = diag(10,0) and the canonical form is 10y_1².

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sqrt{1}0}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−6x1x2+9x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[10000] and P=[−110310310110]
b
D=[300−3] and P=[−15252515]
c
D=[9003] and P=[−15252515]
d
D=[5000] and P=[−12121212]
e
D=[5005] and P=[−12121212]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−3−39]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|1−λ−3−39−λ|=0λ2−10λ=0λ=10,0

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=10, we have A−10I=[1−3−39]−10[1001]=[−9−3−3−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−10I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−13]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=10, we get v1‖v1‖=−110[−13]=[−110310].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[1−3−39]−0[1001]=[1−3−39]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[31]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=10, we get v2‖v2‖=110[31]=[310110].

content.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
content.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sqrt{1}0}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
after.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=10, λ2=1, and λ3=0.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=10, we have A−10I=[240480001]−10[100010001]=[−8404−2000−9]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−10I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[120]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[120].

  • For λ2=1, we have A−I=[240480001]−[100010001]=[140470000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[001]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=1, we get v2‖v2‖=11[001]=[001].

  • For λ3=0, we have A−0I=[240480001]−0[100010001]=[240480001]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[−210]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=5, we get v3‖v3‖=15[−210].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[150−2525015010]

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 3D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
content.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

decision.explanation: Option d has orthonormal columns (0,0,1), (1,1,0)/√2, and (-1,1,0)/√2. They are eigenvectors of A with eigenvalues 2, 0, and -2, respectively. Therefore PᵀAP = D, as required.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
after.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 12
?

A=[−1101−10002],D=[20000000−2]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form Q(x)=xTAx to the canonical (diagonal) form yTDy.

a
[012−2501215100]
b
[012−1210001212]
c
[−1201201012012]
d
[012−1201212100]
e
[120−1201012012]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=2, λ2=0, and λ3=−2.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=2, we have A−2I=[−1101−10002]−2[100010001]=[−3101−30000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[001]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=1, we get v1‖v1‖=11[001]=[001].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[−1101−10002]−0[100010001]=[−1101−10002]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[110]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[110].

  • For λ3=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[−110]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get v3‖v3‖=12[−110].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[012−1201212100]

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d. Its columns (0,0,1), (1,1,0)/√2, and (-1,1,0)/√2 are orthonormal eigenvectors of A with eigenvalues 2, 0, and -2, respectively. Hence PᵀAP = D. The deliberately incorrect submission selected b.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 3D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
content.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
after.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 3D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
content.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

decision.explanation: Option a has orthonormal columns (0,2,1)/√5, (0,-1,2)/√5, and (1,0,0). Multiplication by A gives these columns times 10, 5, and 3, respectively. Therefore PᵀAP = D.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
after.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=5,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=10, λ2=5, and λ3=3.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=10, we have A−10I=[300092026]−10[100010001]=[−7000−1202−4]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−10I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[021]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[021].

  • For λ2=5, we have A−5I=[300092026]−5[100010001]=[−200042021]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−12]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[0−12].

  • For λ3=3, we have A−3I=[300092026]−3[100010001]=[000062023]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[100]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=1, we get v3‖v3‖=11[100]=[100].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[00125−15015250]

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 3D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
content.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=5,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
after.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-3.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 3D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
content.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=1,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-3.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$
